articles.title: 2027 Women's Six Nations: Ireland to host England at Aviva Stadium
articles.summary: Ireland's 2027 Women's Six Nations encounter with England will be played at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.
articles.body:
Ireland's 2027 Women's Six Nations encounter with England will be played at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

Scott Bemand's side made their Six Nations debut at the Aviva Stadium with a win over Scotland in this year's competition and will welcome the world champions to Dublin in the fourth round of fixtures on 8 May.

A crowd of 31,294 watched the 54-5 win over Scotland in May, a record crowd for a women's match in Ireland.

"Playing at Aviva Stadium last season was an incredible and landmark experience for the group and we're really excited to be returning to the home of Irish rugby in 2027," said Ireland captain Erin King.

"These are the occasions you want to be involved in as a player and with two big home matches against France and England coming up in 2027, there is huge motivation for us as a group to produce the occasions and performances that will inspire and excite our Green Wave."

Bemand's side open their campaign in Scotland at Murrayfield on 10 April before they welcome France to the Dexcom Stadium in Galway for their other home fixture of the competition.

Ireland are back on the road in Wales before the Red Roses come to Dublin for the highly anticipated penultimate fixture.

Italy then host the Irish on the final weekend on 15 May.

Ireland finished third in the 2026 Six Nations behind England, who have been champions for the past eight years, and France.

articles.title: James Pater on 'Slim Reaper' nickname and Jonny Wilkinson advice
articles.summary: Northampton teenager James Pater rose slow and stealthy as a prospest, but his opening-day Prem hat-trick has blown the full-back's cover.
articles.body:
Every other year, towards the end of pre-season, Northampton's players are given a pair of smart shoes.

Courtesy of a club sponsor - one of the town's many historic cobblers – each pair is personalised with its new owner's 'Saints number', an individual mark of recognition given to everyone have represented the club's first XV.

James Pater was handed his first set with his number - 2,110 - inscribed on the sole, earlier this month.

On Friday, he showed how well he can fill a pair of shoes.

With club captain George Furbank having moved to Harlequins, Pater was named at full-back for the Prem opener against Newcastle Red Bulls.

The 19-year-old crossed for his first try inside four minutes, scored his second inside 15 and ended the evening with a hat-trick, and the player of the match award, donated to him by original recipient Fin Smith.

It was a start to spur on the hype. Pater's gliding runs and timely support lines have already been attracting admiration for England Under-20s and Saints age-grade sides.

"He's incredibly fast and dynamic. He always looks like he has time on the ball. He reads space exceptionally well, he's strong under the high ball, his passing is top quality, he's not afraid to carry the ball into contact or take defenders on, and he finds gaps you don't think are there."

Pater made similarly stealthy progress as a teenager.

"I always played football growing up," Pater told BBC Sport.

"I didn't start rugby until I went to secondary school and joined Huntingdon Stags.

"Before that it was always football, I played at a high level - Cambridge United's senior development squad. I also played county cricket and some hockey.

"I only got through to Saints academy at 16, which was relatively late. Others were in it from 13 or so. It was coming up to GCSEs and I had to choose to concentrate on something, so I put football to the side."

Around the same time, a star turn helped secure rugby as Pater's priority.

One of the lots in a local charity auction , external was a coaching session with England legend Jonny Wilkinson.

"All the parents from our Shelford Under-16s put £50 in and about 15 of us went down to [England's training base] Pennyhill Park to do a kicking session with him," remembers Pater.

"It was really cool, so fun. I wasn't in the Saints academy then, I just loved played rugby and it wasn't something too serious. But to hear his wisdom was unbelievable."

Last season, Pater played his own starring role in a training session. Before January's Champions Cup meeting with Bordeaux-Begles, Dowson gave Pater the task of replicating mercurial France fly-half Matthieu Jalibert.

"He goes for a lot of chip and chase; little kicks through and likes to create opportunities against unstructured defence," remembers Pater.

"I was just trying to challenge our boys and put people into space."

Pater models his own game more on New Zealand's Beauden Barrett, who shares the versatility to switch between 15 and 10, and Australia's maverick stand-off Quade Cooper.

But at Northampton, inspiration is always close at hand.

"I remember being 17 or 18 in the academy, wanting to make it as a professional and watching Furbs [Furbank], George Hendy and Tommy Freeman tear it up," Pater remembers.

Northampton's production line of talent spins at a dizzying rate. Henry Pollock and Archie McParland - both 21 - are a cohort above Pater, and there is always a new crop of academy prospects blossoming at Franklin's Gardens.

"It's quite [remarkable] actually," says Pater. "Before the Prem Cup game against Saracens [in September], we split into two groups for a warm-up game and I was part of the oldies. I am 19, born July 2007.

"You know there's talent coming through. It keeps everyone keen, wanting the shirt and everyone getting better every day. I like it."

Pater's pre-season goal was to come through that competition and feature in half of Northampton's matchday squads up to Christmas.

The other is to lose a nickname. Weighing 13 and a half stone, Pater was dubbed 'the Slim Reaper' by team-mate Chunya Munga.

Over the summer, building that physique to withstand the rough and tumble of the Prem has been a target.

"I want to be more physically robust, win collisions, challenge people at the gainline and be consistent in playing every Saturday," says Pater

"I'm grinding hard in the gym, I probably have licence to eat whatever I want to put on that weight as well.

"It'll just make me stronger and add to my game, so hopefully it looks better out there when I am running faster and beating people."

Pater, who qualifies for Ireland though his parents and was playing in Ireland's IQ programme , external for eligible overseas prospects before being brought into the England pathway, is not looking too far beyond those goals of establishing himself as a Saints regular.

However, it hasn't escaped his notice either that Pollock's breakthrough season, in which the back row earned senior England and British and Irish Lions selection, came, in terms of academic years, in the equivalent campaign he is in now.

Pater has spoken with England A head coach Mark Mapletoft and the second string have a match against an Argentina XV in November which could be a prime opportunity.

"I don't like to get too far ahead of myself and be arrogant, but obviously I've got goals that I want to achieve," he said.

"But it's all based on performance out on the pitch."

So far, so early in the season, that is only counting in his favour.

articles.title: Tom Curry: England flanker extends contract with Sale Sharks
articles.summary: England international flanker Tom Curry signs a two-year contract extension with Sale Sharks.
articles.body:
England international flanker Tom Curry has signed a two-year contract extension with Sale Sharks.

The 28-year-old has spent his entire career with the Sharks and made his debut aged 18 in October 2016 and his new deal will keep him with the Prem side until the end of the 2027-28 campaign.

Director of rugby Alex Sanderson said Curry, whose identical twin brother Ben also plays for the club, is "fundamental" to the team.

"The terms are a couple of years and that's on Tom's desire to ensure that he's physically in the best spot to be able to honour his contract, to play a load of games for the next two years," Sanderson said.

"Then we both said we'll see where his body's at, at that point, with the want and desire for him to finish his career at Sale.

"He was the one, after some really honest conversations, that said we need to keep this group together, the core group together.

"He's fundamental to us, in terms of being the keystone, really, to that whole group."

Curry added: "Sale Sharks means everything to me and this is the club I have supported my whole life.

"I'm very proud of the hard work we've put in over the last 10 years to get the club to where it is now, but I know how much more we have to give and that's the reason I want to stay. There's no place I would rather be."

Curry, who has been capped 71 times by his country, missed the majority of the 2023-24 season after being diagnosed with femoroacetabular impingement syndrome - a condition that means the ball in the hip joint is not entirely round.

He underwent hip surgery in February 2024 and was warned his career could be over but returned to playing top level rugby just four months later.

In December of that year he had a stem-cell procedure with a view to him being able to play until the 2027 World Cup in Australia.

"He's surpassing expectations, his own medical expectations and what's gone before him in terms of the [hip] injury that he had," Sanderson added.

"We're not seeing any signs of wear and tear at this point and it might come in to factor later down the line but at this point he's as fresh and as mobile as he's ever been."

Change to England selection policy could see Prem 'devalued'

Meanwhile, Sharks summer signing Courtney Lawes, who made his Prem debut for the side in the 34-24 home defeat by Bristol at the weekend, said earlier this month that players who choose to go abroad should remain eligible for England selection.

Lawes, has won 105 England caps and returned to England this summer, having spent two years at French side Brive where he was ineligible to represent his country.

At present, the Rugby Football Union does not permit players not playing in this country to be picked for Steve Borthwick's national side, other than in exceptional circumstances.

Toulouse back row Jack Willis, who has retained his award as the best player in France's Top 14, has not played for England since 2023 but said this week "it's something I still want to do".

However, Exeter Chiefs director of rugby Rob Baxter has said he does not think the rules should be changed and Sanderson said altering the approach could lead to the Prem being "devastated".

"I just think it would devalue our the Prem, which we know is a really good product with really competitive teams, too much if players were allowed to take the pay cheque, move to France and then get the Eurostar over for training with the international team," he said.

"I think it would devastate the Prem because then players can literally have the cake and eat it, can't they? They can take the pay cheque and there'll be no consequence for playing outside of the country.

"I understand the views of those lads who feel otherwise and we have some in our quarters.

"I'm looking at from a different point of view, from a director of rugby that wants the players and we wouldn't be able to compete to keep them on the books if we had to go against some of the juggernauts of the Top 14."

articles.title: Brendan Venter: Saracens' 'wine consultant' misses another press conference
articles.summary: Saracens director of rugby Brendan Venter misses a second pre-match media conference, as head coach Joe Shaw attends.
articles.body:
Saracens head coach Joe Shaw has refused to say when, or if, director of rugby Brendan Venter will speak to the media again, despite the club facing fines for him not doing so.

Venter was not at Wednesday's pre-match press conference for their forthcoming game with Sale after not attending Prem Rugby's pre-season launch day, or doing any media duties before, during or after the opening-weekend victory at Leicester.

The Daily Telegraph reported on Tuesday that Venter had "resigned" as director of rugby and taken up a new role as " head of rugby culture and wine consultant ", but this has not been confirmed by the club nor Prem Rugby.

When asked if Venter would resume media duties, as part of his responsibilities as a director of rugby, Shaw said: "I'm just going to talk about the rugby.

"I'll leave the club to talk about where we stand on all those kind of things."

BBC Sport has contacted Saracens for comment.

It is understood Sarries have already been fined £5,000 after Venter was not present at the Prem's pre-season launch day.

It is also thought a change of job title would not preclude Venter from his contractual responsibilities.

Saracens announced in January that Venter would be returning as director of rugby and have yet to publicly confirm any change to his day-to-day responsibilities.

He succeeded Mark McCall, who stepped down at the end of last season after 15 years in the job.

Shaw confirmed that centre Olly Hartley broke his arm in Sunday's 40-38 win at Leicester.

Hartley, who required full knee reconstruction after a serious injury sustained in a match against Gloucester in April 2024, came off 13 minutes into the match at Welford Road.

Sarries were already 14-0 up but the next 13 minutes after Hartley's injury saw the hosts reduce the deficit to 14-12.

"When you play and train with somebody, like they have been with Olly for so long, and then it's the first game of the season and someone gets properly hurt, breaks their arm, you're human beings, it affects you," Shaw said.

"We managed to to shuffle things around really calmly, with good leadership from the people on the pitch, and it was really pleasing to get through that adversity."

articles.title: Nathan Charles: Former Australia rugby international reveals motor neurone disease diagnosis
articles.summary: Nathan Charles has revealed his motor neurone disease (MND) diagnosis; the 37-year-old made four appearances for Australia across 2014 and 2015; Charles overcame cystic fibrosis to produce a decorated career in professional rugby
articles.body:
The 37-year-old Charles, who made his Test debut in 2014 and earned four caps for the Wallabies, including a 12-12 draw against New Zealand, revealed he has been diagnosed with the same illness as recently retired National Rugby League star Jai Arrow.

MND is an umbrella term for a group of progressive neurological conditions where the motor neurones degenerate. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is the most common form, and ALS is often called Lou Gehrig's disease.

During an interview with former Wallabies lock and now commentator Justin Harrison on Stan Sport this week, Charles revealed he had only recently been diagnosed.

"For a long period there I just didn't know what it was," Charles, who retired from professional rugby in 2018 said."I've had many tests and seen many doctors, but we just weren't getting any answers. My health just kept declining."

"And then recently, in the last few weeks, I was actually diagnosed with motor neurone disease, which has been extremely challenging and overwhelming. I know there's no cure and … your physicality, your body deteriorates and, yeah, your life cuts short."

Charles played Super Rugby for the Perth-based Western Force and Melbourne Rebels, as well as in England with Gloucester, Bath and Wasps. Since retiring, he has served as chief executive of Rugby Western Australia and been involved with Sydney University Rugby Club.

Former England rugby captain and 2003 World Cup winner Lewis Moody was diagnosed with MND last year.

Other high-profile rugby players to have died from the disease in recent years include Rob Burrow and Scottish rugby union great Doddie Weir.

Charles, on his personal website, said he was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis, which primarily affects the lungs and digestive system, when he was three months old and was told he might not live past the age of 10.

"I am constantly pushing the boundaries and am living proof that anything is possible," he said in a post raising awareness of the condition. "It is my personal mission to truly exceed the life expectancy of 37 years [which is the life expectancy of people with CF]."

Now, he said he is trying to deal with a medical setback for which there is currently no cure.

"I was born with a life-threatening illness. I've given that a red-hot crack. Now this other thing comes along," he said. "I find it quite ironic that something else will strike me down rather than what I've been dealing with for my whole life."

The Australian team, who are preparing for Bledisloe Cup Tests against the New Zealand All Blacks this month, posted a message of support on social media.

Wallabies captain Harry Wilson said: "We know you have a tough time ahead, but we're with you on every step of the way."

images.caption: Image: Nathan Charles made four appearances for Australia across 2014 and 2015
